title.en: Yi Shoots Down Nine Suns and Slays the Monsters of the Burned Earth
title.zh: 堯使羿上射十日誅鑿齒

region.en: The scorched Nine Provinces under ten suns (symbolic pin: Central Plains)
region.zh: 十日並出之九州（象徵性定位：中原）

texts.period: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, c. 139 BCE (older Yi cycle in Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing)

source.work: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun: ten suns rise together, the monsters are slain by Yi under Yao's command

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In Yao's reign all ten suns rose together: crops burned, grasses scorched, the people without food. Monsters multiplied — Yayu the man-eater, Zaochi who chiseled teeth, Jiuying of the water-fire, the great wind-bird, the wild boar Fengxi, and the long snake Xiushe. Yao sent Yi of Qiong, who shot down nine suns with the red bow and killed the monsters, and the people rejoiced — Yao was set over the world as Son of Heaven.
summary.zh: 逮至堯之時，十日並出，焦禾稼，殺草木，民無所食；猰貐、鑿齒、九嬰、大風、封豨、修蛇皆為民害。堯使羿誅鑿齒於疇華之野，殺九嬰於凶水之上，繳大風於青丘之澤，斬修蛇於洞庭，禽封豨於桑林——萬民皆喜，堯乃為天子。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi original. Cross-tradition sun-capture cluster (Maui snares the sun); the Chinese version is archery — shooting, not snaring.

passages.text: In the time of Yao, the ten suns came out together. The grain burned in the fields and the grasses and trees were scorched; the people had nothing to eat. And out of the burning world came monsters of every kind: Yayu the man-eater of the west, Zaochi the chisel-toothed giant who slew men with his teeth, and the nine-headed Jiuying of the water and the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, opening (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yao sent for Yi of Qiong, the master archer. Yi shot down the nine lesser suns with the red bow, and each burst into a golden crow and fell; he slew Zaochi in the Wild of Chouhua, killed Jiuying above the Water of Doom, snared the great wind-bird of Qingqiu with a corded arrow, cut off the long snake at Dongting, and took the wild boar Fengxi in the Mulberry Grove.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, Yi's campaign; not verbatim.

passages.text: One sun alone was left, and the sky grew gentle again. The ten thousand people rejoiced and set Yao over them as Son of Heaven, honored as one who had been made emperor in the dark of affliction — the world renewed under a single merciful sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, closing; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins 1993

narrative.en:
China's entry in the sun-capture cluster is the most violent of the world's sun myths: not a snare, not a trick — an execution by archery.

BEGINNING: THE WORLD UNDER TEN SUNS. In the age of Yao the sky's discipline broke. The ten suns, who should have taken the road one at a time from the Fusang tree of the east, rose all together. Ten suns poured down their heat: the grain in the fields burned, the grasses and trees withered, the people were left with nothing to eat. Out of the ruined world came monsters as if the heat itself had bred them — Yayu the man-eater, Zaochi the chisel-toothed slayer, the nine-headed Jiuying breathing water and fire, the great wind-bird that snapped trees and rooftops, the boar Fengxi that gorged in the fields, and the long snake Xiushe that swallowed an elephant in one gulp at Dongting. Humanity was caught between scorching sky and crawling earth.

MIDDLE: THE ARCHER AND HIS BOW. Yao sent for Yi of Qiong, the finest archer of the age — a culture-hero whose bow was of red lacquer, whose arrows were white plumed. Yi climbed the high ground, took aim at the blazing sky, and shot. Nine of the ten suns burst and fell; tradition says each falling sun revealed a great golden crow within, the sun-bird of the Shanhaijing's Fusang cosmology, dropping out of the sky like burning feathers. One sun was left, and it is that one that rises today — spared by mercy, as the tellers always add.

END: THE MONSTERS AND THE RENEWAL. With the sky reduced to order, Yi turned his bow on the earth. He killed Zaochi in the wild of Chouhua, the nine-headed Jiuying above the water of doom, snared the wind-bird at Qingqiu with a line-and-arrow, cut the long snake at Dongting, and caught the boar Fengxi at the Mulberry Grove, where its meat was cooked and offered. The ten thousand people rejoiced, and Yao — who had commanded the deed — was set over the world as Son of Heaven. The burned world was renewed under one sun.

FUNCTION AND AFTERMATH. The story explains why there is only one sun, and why there are droughts (the spared sun's heat is kept in check by ritual — in the Zhuolu cycle, the drought-maid Ba is exorcised). It also founds Yao's sacral kingship: the righter of the sky becomes the model of the sage-ruler. But Yi's own fate is tragic — denied immortality, betrayed by his wife Chang'e (who stole his elixir and flew to the moon), and finally murdered by his student Feng Meng with a peachwood club. The archer's sun-quest, the elixir, and the moon-flight form one continuous cycle of rise, failure, and transformation.
narrative.zh: 十日並出、羿射九日之神話見《淮南子·本經訓》：十日並出，焦禾稼、殺草木，猰貐、鑿齒、九嬰、大風、封豨、修蛇並起為害；堯使羿射九日、誅六害，萬民皆喜，堯乃為天子。此為中國太陽神話之『射日』型——與毛利毛伊縛日平行而以弓箭執行。羿之命運悲劇：不得長生，其妻嫦娥竊藥奔月，羿終為弟子逢蒙以桃杖殺之。射日、靈藥、奔月構成一連續之興衰循環。

functions: Aition of the single sun: why one sun remains and what a second sun costs
Founding of sage-kingship: Yao's mandate confirmed by the ordering of the sky
Agricultural renewal myth: the burned earth restored after monster-clearing
Setup of the elixir and moon-flight cycle (Yi-Chang'e tragedy)

variants.name: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing — the emperor-god Yi
variants.text_tradition: Shanhaijing, Hai Nei Jing (Di Jun's grant of the bow)
variants.summary: An older layer makes Yi the Emperor Di Jun's own red bow granted to a lower heaven, and the suns are shot as birds — the myth as divine prerogative rather than sage-king's commission.

variants.name: Chu Ci, Tianwen — the arrow and the golden crow
variants.summary: The Tianwen asks how Yi shot the suns and why the crows' feathers fell — preserving an archaic version where each sun is a bird that drops its plumage when pierced.

variants.name: Miao/Hmong parallel — the sky too hot
variants.summary: In Miao tellings several suns or moons rise and are shot down by archer-brothers, with surviving sibling suns hiding — an ethnographic parallel suggesting wide distribution of the motif.

primary_sources.citation: c. 139 BCE, Liu An and his court, Huainan; ten-suns passage. Classical Chinese via Wikisource.
Older Yi layer: Di Jun grants the bow; Guo Pu recension.

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — Yi cycle and the archer's tragic arc.
Bodde 1961, in Mythologies of the Ancient World (ed. S. N. Kramer) — the ten-suns motif and drought rituals.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Huainanzi, public-domain Classical Chinese text

title.en: Chang'e Steals the Elixir and Flies to the Moon

region.en: The moon palace (symbolic pin: the moon)

texts.period: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun (c. 139 BCE); elixir narrative via Zhang Heng's Lingxian (2nd c. CE), quoted in later encyclopedias

source.work: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun: Heng'e steals the elixir of Yi and flies to the moon; Zhang Heng, Lingxian: the flight and the moon-toad (quoted in Taiping Yulan)

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Yi, who shot down nine suns, begged the Queen Mother of the West for the drug of immortality; his wife Chang'e (the old reading: Heng'e) stole it, ate it alone, and her body grew light and rose — she flew to the moon, where a cold moon-palace received her, and she became the moon's white toad, keeper of the elixir of the night sky.
summary.zh: 羿請不死之藥於西王母，姮娥竊以奔月，悵然有喪，無以續之；靈憲：嫦娥竊藥奔月，是為蟾蜍——月中蟾宮由是而立。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Huainanzi line and the Lingxian narrative. Name: Han taboo forced Heng'e to be written Chang'e; both forms noted. Cross-tradition quest-immortality cluster.

passages.text: Yi, the archer who had shot down nine suns and saved the world, sought from the Queen Mother of the West the drug of deathlessness. She granted it — one dose, for one man, good for one life beyond all deaths. He brought it home and hid it, meaning to share its power with his wife Chang'e, or to take it himself at the proper season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Huainanzi, Lanming Xun line with the Zhang Heng Lingxian narrative (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chang'e found the elixir and swallowed it entire. Her body grew light as if it had cast off its shadow; she rose from the ground and flew, higher and higher, past the clouds and the winds, until she reached the moon — and could not come back. There in the cold of the moon she looked down at the world she had left, and was stricken with the sorrow of what she had done and what she had become.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Lingxian flight narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: The oldest tellers say she was changed into a toad, the pale toad of the moon, pounding the elixir beneath the cassia tree with the hare. Later ages, pitying her, made the toad only a shadow on the disc, and gave her instead a palace, attendants, and the long loneliness of the Queen of the Moon — the woman who chose to live forever alone rather than die with the man she betrayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of moon-toad and moon-palace traditions; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Compiler's English rendering from the public-domain original; consulted (copyright, summary only): Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins 1993

narrative.en:
The moon-elixir myth is China's quest-immortality tragedy: one drug, two claimants, and a transformation that is both reward and punishment.

BEGINNING: THE DOSE OF DEATHLESSNESS. Yi, the archer of the ten suns, had done the great labor of his age; but culture-heroes are mortal, and Yi knew he would die. He climbed to the far west, to the Jaguar-toothed Queen Mother of the West — the tiger-fanged goddess of calamities who, in the Han, had become keeper of the elixir of life. She granted him the drug: one dose, to be taken in due order. Some tellings say Yi was to share it; some say he hoarded it. Either way, the drug was hidden in his house.

MIDDLE: THE THEFT AND THE FLIGHT. His wife — written Heng'e in the oldest sources, renamed Chang'e when the Emperor Liu Heng's taboo made her name unspeakable — found the elixir. Why she stole it is retold many ways: fear of losing Yi to heaven without her, ambition, anger, or (in the tenderest reading) the wish not to be left mortal when her husband rose. She swallowed it all. The drug of deathlessness lightened her body until it broke the earth's hold; she flew through cloud and wind, up and up, to the moon.

END: THE COLD PALACE AND THE TOAD. The moon received her. The oldest explicit comment, in Zhang Heng's Lingxian, is harsh: in the moon she became a toad — the pale toad of the moon, who pounds the elixir beneath the cassia with the jade hare. Han mirrors carved the toad in the moon's disc. Later ages could not bear the image; they smoothed the toad into a shadow and gave Chang'e a palace of cold jade, attendants, the cassia tree, the hare — and the Mid-Autumn festival, when every household sets out mooncakes and looks up at the woman who traded husband, earth and death for a lonely forever.

FUNCTION. The myth is a cautionary etiology of the moon's nature: cold, bright, untouchable — what happens when the drug of life is taken without measure. It joins the quest-immortality cluster (Gilgamesh's herb lost to the snake; the Hanged God's runes) at the point where the quest is answered but the answer cannot be lived with. And it gives the Chinese moon its population: Chang'e, Yutu the hare, Wu Gang chopping the cassia — all punishments or refusals set into the disc to be watched every year.
narrative.zh: 姮娥奔月之悲劇：一劑不死之藥、二位覬覦者、一場得償所願而無法承受之變形。羿射九日而請藥於西王母；姮娥竊而盡服，身輕離地，飛昇入月；張衡《靈憲》謂其化為蟾蜍——漢鏡鑄月中蟾形；後世不忍其說，遂為月宮、玉兔、桂樹。中秋拜月之俗由此。與吉爾伽美什之草被蛇竊、日耳曼神之祭掛相似：不死之途皆有代價，得之者不得與人世同在。

functions: Etiology of the moon's imagery: toad, hare, cassia, the woman in the disc
Cautionary myth of immortality pursued by theft rather than merit
Ritual anchor of the Mid-Autumn festival (moon-worship, mooncakes, reunion)
Tragic closure of the Yi cycle: the savior-hero loses wife, elixir, and life

variants.name: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun — the bare theft
variants.summary: The earliest surviving telling is one sentence: Heng'e steals the drug Yi asked from the Queen Mother and flees to the moon, grieving, with no way back — the moral ambiguity already present.

variants.name: Zhang Heng, Lingxian — the toad
variants.text_tradition: 2nd c. CE astronomical rhapsody, quoted in later encyclopedias
variants.summary: Adds the transformation into the moon-toad and the flavor of punishment: the elixir-taker becomes the disc's crawling shadow, pounding the drug for the sky.

variants.name: Han-era Chang'e verses — the grief of Yi
variants.text_tradition: Attributed Han-chu song and later poetic tradition
variants.summary: Poetic expansions give Yi's side: left on earth with nothing to continue him, he grieves each full moon; the classical poets (Li Bai, Li Shangyin) keep her sorrow, not her guilt, at the center.

primary_sources.citation: c. 139 BCE; 'Yi begs the elixir from the Queen Mother of the West; Heng'e steals it and flees to the moon.' Classical Chinese via Wikisource.
2nd c. CE; the flight and the moon-toad, preserved in Taiping Yulan quotations.

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — the Yi-Chang'e cycle and the toad variant.

secondary_sources.work: David Leeming, 'A Dictionary of Creation Myths' and lunar myth surveys
secondary_sources.citation: Leeming, various — comparative context of moon-elixir myths.

source_urls.description: Wikisource (zh) — Huainanzi, public-domain Classical Chinese text

title.en: Kun the Fish Becomes Peng the Bird of Ninety Thousand Li

region.en: The Northern Dark (northern ocean) to the Southern Dark (symbolic pin: mythic ocean)
region.zh: 北冥至南冥（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, c. 4th c. BCE; parallel in Liezi, Tang Wen

source.work: Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You (Free and Easy Wandering): Kun and Peng; Liezi, Tang Wen, parallel passage

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: In the Northern Dark lives a fish called Kun, so vast no one knows how many thousand li it is; it changes into a bird called Peng, whose back is like Mount Tai and whose wings hang like clouds from the sky. When the sea moves, the Peng strikes water three thousand li, rises on a whirlwind ninety thousand li, and sets off for the Southern Dark on the six months' wind — while the cicada and the dove laugh at it.
summary.zh: 北冥有魚，其名為鯤，化而為鳥，其名為鵬；背若泰山，翼若垂天之雲；水擊三千里，摶扶搖而上者九萬里，徙於南冥——蜩與學鳩笑之。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Zhuangzi original. Tagging caveat: 'world-serpent' marks the giant-sea-being type (Kun); the Zhuangzi's point is philosophical — scale is relative — rather than combat.

passages.text: In the Northern Ocean there is a fish called Kun; no one knows how many thousand li its body runs. It changes of itself into a bird called Peng, whose back is like the great Mount Tai and whose wings hang from the sky like clouds across the heavens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, Kun-Peng passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sea heaves, the Peng strikes the water for three thousand li, then rises on the whirlwind ninety thousand li high, clears the blue, and sets its face toward the Southern Ocean on the wind of six months. The cicada and the little dove laugh at it: 'We hop from tree to tree — what does that creature think it needs all that height for?' The great and the small, says Zhuangzi, know their own limits, and that is the whole difference between them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Xiaoyao You, with the cicada-and-dove commentary; not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Hundun, Chaos Given Seven Holes

region.en: The South Sea and North Sea, meeting at the center (symbolic pin: central plain)
region.zh: 南海北海之中央（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang chapter, c. 4th c. BCE

source.work: Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang (The Normal Course for Rulers and Kings): Shu and Hu drill seven holes in Hundun

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The kings of the South Sea (Shu) and North Sea (Hu) met regularly in the land of Hundun, the central chaos, who treated them well; to repay him they decided to give him the senses everyone else had, and each day they bored one hole — seven days, seven holes — and on the seventh day Hundun died. Unity, given features, ceases to be itself.
summary.zh: 南海之帝為儵，北海之帝為忽，中央之帝為混沌；儵忽遇於混沌之地，報其德而欲鑿七竅——日鑿一竅，七日而混沌死。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Zhuangzi original. Links to the Shanhaijing's faceless god Dijiang (chinese-shanhaijing-dijiang); the parable is anti-civilizing in Zhuangzi's hands.

passages.text: The emperor of the South Sea was Shu, and the emperor of the North Sea was Hu, and the emperor of the middle was Hundun — the undivided one, who had no face. Shu and Hu often met in Hundun's land, and Hundun treated them very well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang, Hundun parable (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: They wished to repay his kindness, and reasoned that all men have seven openings — eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth — by which they see, hear, eat and breathe; Hundun alone had none. Each day they bored one hole in him. On the seventh day, the seventh hole was finished, and Hundun died. The undivided whole, given the features of the divided world, ceases to exist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Zhuangzi, Yinglei Diwang, seven-holes passage; not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant of Longbo Hooks Away the Turtles of Penglai

region.en: The five sacred isles far off in the Gulf of Bohai (symbolic pin: Bohai Sea)
region.zh: 渤海之東五神山（象徵性定位：渤海）

texts.period: Liezi, Tang Wen chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Tang Wen (Questions of Tang): the five isles, the sixteen giant turtles, and the fisher-giant of Longbo

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Five magic isles floated without anchor in the eastern sea, and fifteen great turtles bore them on their backs in shifts; the giant of Longbo country strode the deep sea, hooked six turtles with a single cast, carried them home on his back to divine by the shells — and Daiyu and Yuanjiao, left drifting, drifted north and sank, so the gods had to relocate Penglai's survivors and forbid further wandering by giants.
summary.zh: 渤海之東有五山，常隨波上下，帝命禺疆使巨鰲十五舉首而戴之；龍伯之國大人一釣而連六鰲，負之馳歸，灼其骨以卜——岱輿、員嶠流於北極，沉於大海，仙聖播遷；帝怒，侵減龍伯之國使阨。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. The giant's casual fishing trip as cosmic catastrophe — trickster-scale humor.

passages.text: East of the Gulf of Bohai, far beyond the horizon, five sacred isles — Daiyu, Yuanjiao, Fanghu, Yingzhou, Penglai — floated on the waves without anchor, for they had no fixed ground beneath them; the immortals who lived there dreaded their drifting. So the High Emperor ordered the sea-god Yuqiang to command fifteen great turtles, who took the isles on their heads in shifts of sixty thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, five-isles passage (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: But in the country of Longbo there lived giants taller than mountains. One of them, on a whim, strode into the deep sea, cast a line, and hooked six of the turtles at once; he slung them on his back and ran home to his own country, where he burned their shells to divine the future. Daiyu and Yuanjiao, losing their bearers, drifted to the far north and sank beneath the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, Longbo fishing episode; not verbatim.

passages.text: The immortals of the sunken isles were scattered, migrating in exile. The High Emperor was furious: he diminished the Longbo country to a few thousand li, and shrank its giants to a few feet — and so the surviving isles of Penglai and its sisters stand in the eastern sea to this day, and no giant wanders the deep again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, punishment and aftermath; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fool of the North Moves Two Mountains

region.en: Between Taihang and Wangwu, north of the Yellow River bend (symbolic pin: Shanxi–Henan border)
region.zh: 太行王屋二山（象徵性定位：晉豫交界）

texts.period: Liezi, Tang Wen chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Tang Wen (Questions of Tang): Yugong, ninety years old, moves Taihang and Wangwu

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ninety-year-old Yugong summoned his household to dig away the two mountains that blocked his road to the south, bucket by bucket, generation by generation — 'my sons will have sons; the mountains grow no taller.' The Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughed at him; Yugong answered, and the gods of the mountains, afraid, asked the Emperor of Heaven, who ordered the two sons of Kuae's giant to carry the mountains away on their backs — one to the east, one to the south.
summary.zh: 太行、王屋二山方七百里，懲山北之塞出入之迂；愚公年九十，率子孫荷擔者三夫，叩石墾壤，箕畚運於渤海之尾——子子孫孫無窮匱也，而山不加增。操蛇之神懼，帝感其誠，命夸娥氏二子負二山。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. The parable became a 20th-century Chinese political byword (Mao's 'Three Fairy Tales' speech) — noted as modern reception, not part of the mythic record.

passages.text: The two mountains Taihang and Wangwu blocked Yugong's household from the southern roads, a round trip of months. At ninety years, Yugong called his family together and proposed to dig away the mountains: they would carry the earth and stone, basket by basket, to the far shore of the Bohai Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, Yugong opening (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wise Old Man of the River Bend came to laugh at him — an old man with months to live, against mountains seven hundred li around. Yugong answered: though I die, my son lives on; my sons will have sons, and sons will have sons, without end — but the mountain can add nothing to itself. Why should it not be leveled? The mountain-god, holding a snake, trembled at the resolve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, the dispute with the Wise Old Man; not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods of the two mountains, afraid, reported Yugong's resolve to the Emperor of Heaven, whose heart was moved by such constancy. He ordered the two sons of Kuae's giant to shoulder the mountains, one on each man's back, and set the one east of Shuofang and the other south of Yongzhou — and from that day, no hill stood between Yugong's house and the roads of the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Tang Wen, divine intervention; not verbatim.

title.en: Yanshi Presents King Mu with a Mechanical Man

region.en: King Mu's western tour, beyond the Kunlun passes (symbolic pin: Hexi corridor)
region.zh: 穆王西巡昆侖之丘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Liezi, Mu Wang Pian chapter, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE

source.work: Liezi, Mu Wang Pian (Treatise on King Mu): the craftsman Yanshi and his walking, singing automaton

texts.license: Public domain (Classical Chinese text; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Returning from his westward tour, King Mu was met by the craftsman Yanshi, who presented a man that walked, looked, sang and danced like a living being. At the height of the dance it winked at the king's ladies; Mu was furious — until Yanshi took the figure apart before him: skin, flesh, sinews, joints, heart, liver, intestines — all leather, wood, glue and paint, reassembled by night, and the machine sang again.
summary.zh: 偃師造能唱能舞之假人；其倡也，瞬其目而招王之左右侍妾——王大怒；偃師立剖散之：皆傅會革、木、膠、漆，內則肝膽心肺、腸胃外則筋骨支節——試廢其心則口不能言，廢其肝則目不能視。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the Liezi original. One of the world's oldest automaton tales; tagged 'quest-immortality' loosely for the King Mu elixir-tour frame, noted as interpretive.

passages.text: Returning from his journey to the west, King Mu of Zhou was met on the road by a craftsman called Yanshi, who asked for an audience and brought with him a man. 'This is my work,' said Yanshi — and the man could walk, could look about, could nod and bow, and when Yanshi sang it sang, and when he danced it danced, in a thousand varieties of movement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, Yanshi episode (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king watched with his favorite ladies beside him — and at the height of the dance the automaton winked its eye at them. Mu raged and called it sorcery; Yanshi, terrified, took the figure apart on the spot before the king: inside there was nothing but leather, wood, glue and paint — organs of leather and timber, joints and sinews of cord — all artificial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, the wink and the disassembly; not verbatim.

passages.text: Yanshi put it together again, and it moved and sang as before. Then, to test it, the king removed its heart — and its mouth could not speak; the liver — and its eyes could not see; the kidneys — and its feet could not walk. Mu exclaimed that human craft could equal the Creator's: he had the automaton loaded on the rear carriage and carried back to his capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Liezi, Mu Wang Pian, organ-removal test; not verbatim.
